title: Acyl substitution: add, then kick out

steps.text: Acid derivatives get attacked just like ketones in pattern A: a nucleophile adds to the C=O carbon and the π electrons go up onto oxygen. The difference is a **leaving group** on that carbon. So the O⁻ comes back down, the C=O re-forms, and the leaving group is pushed out. Add, then eliminate: that is pattern B.
Methyl acetate is an ester. Tap the atom of its **leaving group** that is bonded to the C=O carbon.
steps.explain: The single-bonded oxygen leaves, taking CH3 with it as methoxide (CH3O⁻). The C=O oxygen stays: it is the one that takes the electrons up and pushes them back down.

steps.text: Acid derivatives sit on a **reactivity ladder**: acid chloride > anhydride > ester ≈ carboxylic acid > amide. The better the leaving group (Cl⁻ is best, ⁻NH2 is worst), the more reactive the derivative. Substitution runs downhill: a more reactive derivative turns into a less reactive one, not the other way.
Which conversion works in one step?

options.explains: That's uphill. Even if Cl⁻ added, the intermediate would just push out Cl⁻ again, because Cl⁻ is the better leaving group. A nucleophile can't replace a group that leaves worse than it does.
Amides are the bottom rung. ⁻NHCH3 is a terrible leaving group, so methanol can't push it out. Amides need strong acid or base and heat even to hydrolyse.
Downhill on the ladder: Cl⁻ is a much better leaving group than CH3O⁻, so the ester is the more stable product. (Going up needs a special reagent, like SOCl2 to turn an acid into an acid chloride.)
Uphill again: acetate is a worse leaving group than chloride, so the acid chloride can't form this way. You only go down the ladder.

steps.text: The key step is the addition: O attacks C, and the C=O π bond goes up to O. Right after, the O⁻ comes back down and Cl⁻ leaves.
Same move on an anhydride. The attack is drawn; add the arrow that finishes the addition.
A ketone adds a nucleophile and stops at the alkoxide (pattern A). **Why** does an ester's tetrahedral intermediate collapse instead?

options.text: Esters are more electrophilic than ketones, so they react further.
options.explains: Esters are actually less electrophilic than ketones: the OR oxygen donates electrons into the C=O. Reactivity doesn't decide this; having a leaving group does.

options.text: The ester carbon carries a group that can leave as a fairly stable anion (CH3O⁻), so the O⁻ pushes it out and the strong C=O re-forms.
options.explains: Right. The leaving group is the whole difference between pattern A and pattern B.

options.text: Ketones collapse too, but they lose H⁻ or R⁻ instead.
options.explains: H⁻ and R⁻ are far too basic to leave. That's exactly why ketones stop at the alkoxide and get protonated on workup.

options.text: The nucleophile falls off again, so the ester comes back.
options.explains: That would just return the starting material. Here the group that leaves is the OR, not the nucleophile that came in.

steps.text: Methyl pentanoate is treated with (1) LiAlH4, then H3O+, or (2) **DIBAL-H** at −78 °C, then H2O. What do you get?

options.explains: Swapped. LiAlH4 is the strong, unselective one; DIBAL-H at low temperature is the one that stops at the aldehyde.

options.text: Both give pentanal: one hydride per ester.
options.explains: With LiAlH4 the aldehyde forms while hydride is still around, and aldehydes are more reactive than esters, so it gets reduced too.
This misses the low-temperature trick: DIBAL-H's intermediate doesn't collapse to the aldehyde until water is added, when no hydride is left to reduce it.

LiAlH4 adds hydride, CH3O⁻ leaves, and the aldehyde formed is more reactive than the ester, so it is reduced again to the 1° alcohol. DIBAL-H gives one hydride, and at −78 °C its tetrahedral intermediate holds together until workup, when it falls apart to the aldehyde.
